subject: Humanities
objective_verbatim: Place key protest/rights events on a timeline (chronology).

GROW Weekly - Spring.C40: Place key protest/rights events on a timeline (chronology).
GROW Weekly - Spring.D40_to_F40_generic: Enquiry into protest, civil rights, suffrage and social reform using suitable sources. Formative source tasks. Later structured historical account and source evaluation.

historical_name_rule: Public historical people, events, places and dates may be named. No living private identities, pupils, staff, school/local identifiers, website addresses or reproduced historical text.

events.title: Some women gain the vote
events.summary: A UK law let some women aged 30 or over vote. Many women still could not vote.
events.staff_precision: The Representation of the People Act 1918 received Royal Assent on 6 February 1918. Women aged at least 30 needed qualifying electoral/property status, or qualifying husbands. Most men aged at least 21 could vote, with younger service voters also eligible. This was not equal voting rights for all women.

events.title: Montgomery bus boycott begins
events.summary: Black people and their supporters stopped using buses in Montgomery. They aimed to end rules that kept Black and White riders apart.
events.staff_precision: This is the boycott start, not Rosa Parks's arrest on 1 December 1955. The boycott challenged racial segregation on buses. No arrest or violence scene is reproduced.

events.title: March on Washington
events.summary: People marched in Washington, DC, to call for jobs and equal rights. It was a peaceful mass protest.
events.staff_precision: March on Washington for Jobs and Freedom, 28 August 1963. No speeches or signs are reproduced. Participants held many roles in a movement, rather than a single person's achievement.

events.title: Civil Rights Act becomes law
events.summary: A US law banned unfair race rules in many public places and at work. People still had to act to make the law work.
events.staff_precision: Civil Rights Act signed into law on 2 July 1964. It prohibited segregation in public accommodations and employment discrimination. Avoid claiming every form of discrimination ended or law alone instantly changed daily life.

events.title: Voting Rights Act becomes law
events.summary: A US law helped protect the right to vote. It aimed to stop unfair rules that kept Black voters out.
events.staff_precision: Voting Rights Act signed into law on 6 August 1965. It strengthened federal protection against racial discrimination in voting. Legal rights still required implementation and enforcement.

source_card_status: Teacher-written factual summaries for learning. These are not historical quotations, testimony or archive extracts.
model_status: Illustrative teacher-written teaching model. It is attributed to no real person.
model_text: I look at the year first. 1918 comes before 1955, so E1 goes before E2. I then check the other years. 1963 comes before 1964 and 1965. I keep each date with its event. The five places on this strip show order. They do not show equal gaps in time.
timeline_representation: Ordinal order in equal-sized boxes; not proportional time gaps. 1918 to 1955 is a gap of 37 calendar years.

Supported: Use all five event cards and the year mat. An adult may read the cards. Find the smallest year first.
Build your own strip of five in your book. Use one date-and-event label at a time. Check it before adding the next.
Point, say or write one reason with this frame: ____ comes before ____ because ____ is the earlier year.
Independent: Read all five cards. Sort the complete date-and-event pairs from earliest to latest. Check all years.
Make your own strip of five in your book. Keep the date and title together. Check each one against the source card.
Explain one place using a date. Say what the equal-sized boxes do and do not show about time gaps.
Aspire: Build and check your own five-event strip. Keep every date and event together.
Work out the gap in calendar years from 1918 to 1955. Does equal spacing on the strip show that real gap? Explain.
Test a new date pair from the same year: 2 July 1964 and 28 August 1964. Explain how months settle the order. These extra dates are date practice, not extra event cards.

success_criteria: I can match each event to its date.
I can put all five events from earliest to latest.
I can use a date to explain one place on my timeline.

hinge.question: Which comes first: 5 December 1955 or 28 August 1963? Explain what you checked first.
hinge.answer: 5 December 1955 comes first because 1955 is the earlier year. The year comes before the month when comparing different years.
hinge.rule: Ask each pupil privately. If a pupil orders August before December without checking years, model the year check and use the parallel question before independent work.
hinge.parallel: Which comes first: 28 August 1963 or 2 July 1964? Answer: 28 August 1963, because 1963 comes before 1964.

pair_work: Date Finder chooses a date and says which year comes first. Event Checker keeps the date and event together and checks the source card. Swap after one turn. Each pupil then makes an individual five-event strip.
finish: In your book, make your own strip of all five events. Use the cut-out labels or write five date-and-event pairs. Put the earliest first. Check each pair against its card. Add one sentence: ____ comes before ____ because ____.
sensitive_pause: Use the agreed quiet signal to ask the adult for a pause. Use the usual supervised place. No public reason is needed. Rejoin with one date check or a private recap. A neutral task with number cards is available.

evidence.description: Own five complete date-event pairs in chronological order and one date-based reason. Actual help and individual understanding recorded.

communication: Offer to the Communication portfolio. Voice, adult audience reply, one NS and own response precede R. E follows actual banking.

resources.Staff_Answers.docx:
Staff answers for the five event timeline
Friday 8 January 2027 | P2 | 40 minutes | Year A
Humanities | GROW | Spring 1 Week 1 | HUM-GROW-S1-W01
Expected order: E1, E2, E3, E4, E5. Keep every full date paired with its event. Accept pupils’ own equivalent wording that preserves the event and its historical limits.
Card and date
Event and precision
E1
6 February 1918
Some women gain the vote. The Representation of the People Act 1918 received Royal Assent on 6 February 1918. Women aged at least 30 needed qualifying electoral/property status, or qualifying husbands. Most men aged at least 21 could vote, with younger service voters also eligible. This was not equal voting rights for all women.
E2
5 December 1955
Montgomery bus boycott begins. This is the boycott start, not Rosa Parks's arrest on 1 December 1955. The boycott challenged racial segregation on buses. No arrest or violence scene is reproduced.
E3
28 August 1963
March on Washington. March on Washington for Jobs and Freedom, 28 August 1963. No speeches or signs are reproduced. Participants held many roles in a movement, rather than a single person's achievement.
E4
2 July 1964
Civil Rights Act becomes law. Civil Rights Act signed into law on 2 July 1964. It prohibited segregation in public accommodations and employment discrimination. Avoid claiming every form of discrimination ended or law alone instantly changed daily life.
E5
6 August 1965
Voting Rights Act becomes law. Voting Rights Act signed into law on 6 August 1965. It strengthened federal protection against racial discrimination in voting. Legal rights still required implementation and enforcement.
Valid before and after reasons
E1 comes before E2 because 1918 is earlier than 1955. E2 comes before E3 because 1955 is earlier than 1963. E3 comes before E4 because 1963 is earlier than 1964. E4 comes before E5 because 1964 is earlier than 1965. Accept any accurate pair in either direction with its correct date comparison.
Gap and same year extension
1955 minus 1918 equals 37 calendar years. The exact elapsed interval between 6 February 1918 and 5 December 1955 is more than 37 years; this task asks for the difference in calendar years. Equal-sized strip boxes do not represent equal time gaps. For date practice, 2 July 1964 precedes 28 August 1964 because July comes before August in the same year. These practice dates add no extra historical event.

Answer checks feedback and historical limits
Friday 8 January 2027 | P2 | 40 minutes | Year A
Humanities | GROW | Spring 1 Week 1 | HUM-GROW-S1-W01
After the model
E3, 28 August 1963, comes before E4, 2 July 1964. The pupil should compare 1963 and 1964 first. An exact adult reading of the dates gives access; an instruction to put E3 first is a chronology prompt and must be recorded as such.
Hinge and parallel check
Which comes first: 5 December 1955 or 28 August 1963? Explain what you checked first.
5 December 1955 comes first because 1955 is the earlier year. The year comes before the month when comparing different years.
Ask each pupil privately. If a pupil orders August before December without checking years, model the year check and use the parallel question before independent work.
Which comes first: 28 August 1963 or 2 July 1964? Answer: 28 August 1963, because 1963 comes before 1964.
Misconceptions and corrections
1 Months before years: a learner may place August 1963 before December 1955 because August comes earlier in a year. Return to the year fields and compare 1955 with 1963. Only compare months when the years match.
2 Equal spacing means equal gaps: the five boxes are positions in an ordered list. They are not a scaled timeline. The calendar-year differences are 37, 8, 1 and 1. Do not present their equal printed widths as elapsed time.
Additional historical precision: the 1918 law enfranchised some women aged at least 30 under qualifying conditions. The bus boycott began on 5 December 1955. The 1964 and 1965 laws required implementation and did not instantly remove every form of discrimination. These events are selected examples, not a complete rights history or proof that one single protest caused every later law.
Judging individual evidence
Require all five date-and-event pairs in order and one date-based before/after reason across all routes. A pupil may direct the strip or use a scribe. Retain the exact directed response and actual history prompts. Class sorting alone is insufficient for individual evidence. Do not infer independent reading from an adult-read card.
Offer to the Communication portfolio. Keep the learner’s own voice, an actual audience reply and one NS, then the learner’s response in the same colour, on the same page or usual mode before recording R. Record E only after actual evidence banking. A shared class answer does not establish each learner’s understanding.
Sensitive history and provenance
Present the impact of racist rules clearly without asking pupils to experience them through seating, labels or role play. No personal disclosure or public answer is required. Use the agreed supervised pause route. All card text is teacher-written factual summary, with no reproduced archive text, testimony or speech. Models are illustrative and attributed to no real person.
Research basis: UK Parliament, The Representation of the People Act 1918; US National Archives, The Montgomery Bus Boycott, The March on Washington for Jobs and Freedom, Civil Rights Act, July 2, 1964, and Voting Rights Act (1965). Library of Congress, The Bus Boycott, provides a cross-check. Dates and statutory scope are summarised in the source record. No website address is supplied.
resources.TA_Brief.docx:
TA brief for the five event timeline
Friday 8 January 2027 | P2 | 40 minutes | Year A
Humanities | GROW | Spring 1 Week 1 | HUM-GROW-S1-W01
GROW group of up to five. Outcome: Place key protest/rights events on a timeline (chronology).
Before the lesson
Prepare all five Event_Cards, Timeline_Strips, books and ready-cut date-and-event labels. Offer White or Pink print and usual aids. Agree the discreet pause signal and familiar supervised place. Keep the final individual strip separate from the class sort.
I do and check
Direct attention to the year while the teacher models E1 before E2. An adult may read the exact card wording as access. After the model, each pupil checks whether 28 August 1963 comes before 2 July 1964. Answer: yes, because 1963 is earlier. Record separately any cue that supplies an ordering answer.
We do and hinge
Date Finder checks the date. Event Checker keeps it with the event. Rotate and swap roles across the group. Check each pupil privately: 5 December 1955 or 28 August 1963 first? Answer: December 1955, by year. If months lead the decision, point back to years, then check 28 August 1963 before 2 July 1964.
Independent and review
Every pupil builds their own five-event strip in their book, with one before/because reason. Accept directed placement, typing or exact scribing. Expected order E1, E2, E3, E4, E5. Check date and title together. The boxes show order only. Aspire: the 1918-to-1955 calendar-year gap is 37. Give one NS and keep the pupil’s own response before R. E follows actual banking only.
Planned access and calm participation
Cognition: one card, year mat, faded model. Communication: short instruction, quiet rehearsal and processing time. SEMH: predictable turns, no forced public answer or disclosure. Sensory/Physical: enlarged or ready-cut labels and usual aids. EAL: plan in any language and use word support. Prompt ladder: 1) Point to place/instruction. 2) Ask short question. 3) Rephrase instruction. 4) Provide scaffold/choice. 5) Model first step only, then return task.
Use the agreed supervised pause route without a public explanation. Neutral task: order 1, 3, 2, 5, 4. Rejoin through one private date check. No racism simulation, historical role play or discriminatory seating. Correct racist language calmly and follow existing safeguarding arrangements for concerns.

Theme: Resilience & Change. Unit: Protest, rights & change. These five events in the UK and the United States are a short selection, not a complete history of rights. Today checks chronology through formative source tasks; no qualification or award completion is inferred.

Cognition and Learning
Use explicit year-first modelling, one card at a time and a worked example that fades. Keep all five events in the final task. Give the year mat or a sentence frame without supplying the order. Use a quick check after the model to decide whether to reteach.

Use a predictable sequence and private feedback. Preview racism and unequal rights factually and calmly. If covering this lesson
Read the previous three pages and Staff_Answers before teaching. Use the supplied cards rather than adding live resources or quotations. Model one comparison only, lead the shared sort, then give every pupil time for their own five-event strip. If the projector fails, read exact card wording and model with the printed cards on the table. The same outcome and evidence apply.
Keep each date attached to its event throughout. If a pupil cannot cut or write, let them direct label placement or dictate an exact date-and-title sequence. Record what the pupil decided and what the adult did. If a pupil remains paused, preserve the unfinished status and arrange a calm later opportunity; do not infer completion.
Common errors to correct
Months before years: August is earlier in a year than December, but August 1963 is later than December 1955. Compare the year first, then month and day only when needed. Equal boxes: the strip shows event order, not equal elapsed time. The first calendar-year gap is 37 years, not the same as the later gaps.
Do not say all women gained equal voting rights in 1918, or that a rights law instantly ended discrimination. E2 is the start of the bus boycott on 5 December 1955, not the arrest four days earlier. Chronology shows order; order alone does not prove one event caused another.

Stage Reference, 0 minutes.
Reference answer slide: reveal after the class card sort and each pupil's own strip, when checking or at review. Equal-sized boxes/rows show sequence, not equal intervals. The interval from 1918 to 1955 is 37 calendar years. The complete dates, not year labels alone, stay attached to each event. E1: The Representation of the People Act 1918 received Royal Assent on 6 February 1918. Women aged at least 30 needed qualifying electoral/property status, or qualifying husbands. Most men aged at least 21 could vote, with younger service voters also eligible. This was not equal voting rights for all women.
E2: This is the boycott start, not Rosa Parks's arrest on 1 December 1955. The boycott challenged racial segregation on buses. No arrest or violence scene is reproduced.
E3: March on Washington for Jobs and Freedom, 28 August 1963. No speeches or signs are reproduced. Participants held many roles in a movement, rather than a single person's achievement.
E4: Civil Rights Act signed into law on 2 July 1964. It prohibited segregation in public accommodations and employment discrimination. Avoid claiming every form of discrimination ended or law alone instantly changed daily life.
E5: Voting Rights Act signed into law on 6 August 1965. It strengthened federal protection against racial discrimination in voting. Legal rights still required implementation and enforcement.
These five events are selected examples. They do not imply one continuous campaign across two countries or that protests automatically produced the next law.
